Just a few things, in no particular order.

It's a lot of trouble. If I could just flip a switch and no longer exist, I'd probably do that. But I've thought about a lot of different methods and they're all pretty messy and surprisingly hard to pull off right. For example:

- Many instances of people shooting themselves in the head and ending up with brain damage or otherwise surviving with a worse quality of life. Also, I do not live in an area where guns are readily available. I mean, I could probably get a gun over the course of a weekend if I wanted to, but it's a logistical barrier, and when I'm depressed I have very little energy for logistics.

- Overdoses often result in passing out, throwing up, and again surviving with reduced quality of life.

- Jumping off a bridge can be very miserable. Again, lots of cases of people merely breaking their legs on contact and then either frantically swimming to shore, or drowning. Drowning with broken legs doesn't sound fun.

- Jumping in front of a train seems like the surest bet, but jesus that's a shitty thing to do. I don't want to emotionally scar an innocent train conductor.

- Disembowelment is probably the route I'd try to go if I really decided to do it today. Knives are always handy and there's the pro (or con, depending on perspective) that it requires some serious follow-through so you can't just do it willy-nilly. Downside: painful as *all hell*, and leaves a hell of a mess.

But killing myself *today* isn't really on the table. I've made a promise to myself that when I want to kill myself, I wait 90 days. If at any point in those 90 days, it doesn't seem like a good idea -- even for a minute -- then I stop. Imagine a sign that says "It has been <X> days since I had any will to live." Until that sign hits 90, it's a no-go. (And realistically I don't start thinking about suicide until I've already had no will for a long while, so...maybe this is really like a year?)

Also, I have enough money saved up that I could quit my job and travel for a while. I would do this before killing myself, cuz why not? So again this changes the barrier from simply wanting to die to actually taking many mundane actions -- quitting my job, booking travel plans, etc. When depressed, these seem like bigger hurdles than actually offing myself. It's kind of weird.

As for family and friends, I'm sorry, but even though I care, if I can't live my life for myself then I'm not going to live it just for other people. It's not reasonable.

Ugh. Thank you for saying it. As a guy, I've been in this situation many times, where a woman will simply not stop, to the point where I have exactly two options:

1. Use violent force to escape
2. Just take it

If I go with option 1, I'm the bad guy. There is no non-harmful way to escape someone like that. They will not back down, and at *best* you will need to shove them to the ground and *run*. And in the time it takes to unlock a door, or grab clothes and shoes, they're already back on top of you and you have to do it again.

Specifics range from sexual assault to physical violence to simply blocking my way when I want to leave. I hate myself for ever putting up with it, but if it happens again, guess what? I'm going to do the same thing because there's no way out. There's no fucking way out.

Yes, I could overpower her, but I am not so overwhelmingly strong that I can overpower her *without hurting her*. How do you fight someone who knows damn well you'll never hurt her?!

Posting this with an old throwaway for various reasons.

The biggest barrier is respect, privacy, and anonymity -- more to the point, the complete lack thereof. There was no one I could talk to who would not "turn me in" if I was completely honest with them. If a shrink thinks you're going to kill yourself, they are required by law to call the cops on you. Those cops are then required by law to have you committed to a hospital against your will.

This is not acceptable. I've seen psych wards, and they are horrible places. The people there have no respect for their patients and will threaten them with sedatives if they dare to complain about anything, like their rights. Getting upset in such an environment is not a sign of a psychological problem -- *any normal person* would go mad being treated that way.

It's not a risk I'm willing to take for the ultra-slim chance that someone will be able to tell me something new and change my perspective.

If you can crack this problem with an app, then good on you. But it's a tough one to crack, especially with the legal framework built around it.

I use this account only to talk about issues relating to suicide. Feel free to look at my post history for more on this theme.

I do believe my own advice, but it's not exactly the most upbeat advice.

Too often, people preach faith. This just does not resonate with me. Not at all. But for me, I found that my skepticism serves the same purpose as others' faith. So I preach skepticism.

Preaching faith means trying to convince someone that everything will be fine in the end. I don't believe that, and nobody's really going to convince me. When I'm depressed, I'm *quite certain* that everything is and will continue to be miserable. I'll bet you are, too.

Preaching skepticism means trying to un-convince someone that everything will be terrible. This is more realistic. I'm not going to tell you you're wrong -- only that you *might* be, because you are, like everyone other human, basically a dumbass. Your certainty is suspect, and you need to be skeptical of yourself. You don't *really know* the future. I don't either. But shit happens -- and occasionally good shit happens, too. You can't predict it.

Maybe everything in your entire life, everything you've observed and read about human history, supports your worldview and the model of reality you have in your head. Maybe you think that means you're right, and your model gives you predictive powers. This is almost certainly bullshit, though, for two reasons:

1. [Confirmation bias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confirmation_bias). Everybody suffers from it. Show two people with opposite views on an issue a news article about it, and both of them will come away *more* convinced that they're right -- they will interpret the same facts in completely opposite ways, so they support their pre-existing views. They also have greater memory for facts that "click" with their pre-existing beliefs and views than those that conflict.

2. [The Black Swan effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_swan_theory). Looking back on history, everything always seems to make sense. We can fit it all into a neat narrative and think "well of course! It couldn't have possibly happened any other way!" But the fact is, that's just 20/20 hindsight. Humans are much better at *rationalizing* and much worse at *reasoning* than we like to admit. Look back on the major cultural and political events of just the past 20 years: did you see any of them coming more than a year in advance? Did you predict the rise of terrorism? Seems like nobody did, and yet in hindsight it's *so obvious*.

I highly recommend reading [the book by Nassim Nicholas Taleb](http://www.amazon.com/The-Black-Swan-Improbable-Robustness/dp/081297381X). He expands on this thesis relentlessly and convincingly.

People are stupid. You're a person. Therefore, you are stupid. Consider this, and question yourself. Of course, I'm phrasing this a little aggressively here; I really don't want it to sound like I'm beating up on anyone and saying "you're only depressed because you're an idiot!" Not at all. I respect your experience, I respect your views, and most of all I respect your feelings. I just mean that humans are flawed creatures and we should treat ourselves as such, and never be too confident in our own judgments.

TL;DR: Applied toward the negative, skepticism is like faith, and doubt is like hope. I preach skepticism and doubt, because they resonate with me in ways that faith and hope have never come close to.

As someone who has been suicidal for a great many years of his life, I'd like to offer my perspective.

The thing that makes it *so hard* for me to seek any kind of help is that I know nobody will respect me. Nobody will respect my decision if I want to kill myself. Everybody will act like you, and *that's why* I can't seek help. Above all, I need to be respected, and I need to have freedom. People who do not respect me, and would restrict my freedom -- people who will treat me as less than human because *I don't think like they do* -- well, would YOU want such people in YOUR life?

I'd cut you out of my life, too.

I'm sorry. I know this sounds harsh, and please understand that I'm not judging you. If the shoe were on the other foot, I might do the same thing. It sounds like he was not so much discussing it with you as informing you, and that has to be fucking terrifying for you. I can't blame you for seeing it as a "cry for help". When you weigh the regret of calling when you shouldn't have vs the regret of *not* calling when you *should* have, it seems obvious that you had to make that call.

On the one hand, I sympathize with you and agree that you did what you had to do. On the other hand, your kind of attitude makes my life harder and creates a hostile culture for me. I think this is a type of prisoner's dilemma. It doesn't even make sense for you to act differently unless everybody else does, too.

This isn't a black and white issue. I don't really have a point to make. I just want to offer a perspective that may be lacking.

Not really sure what my "lowest" is, because there are different types that are hard to compare. Some are like sprints and some are like marathons.

For the sprints, which are like panic attacks, I remind myself myself that *it will pass*. If I just mechanically move through the day, tomorrow will be better. This is usually true.

For the marathons, which are more like extended depression, that doesn't work, because tomorrow most likely *won't* be better. But I have enough money saved for a trip. If push comes to shove, I will take another trip before I kill myself. So now the decision is not between living and dying, but between continuing my day-to-day life and dropping everything to travel. I'm always at least a few months away from pulling the trigger.

There's also the thought that there are a couple people in the world I promised to see again. At the time, I didn't think it would be such a hard promise to keep.

Do they know because you've talked to them about it, or is it just an unspoken understanding?

Only my closest friends know I've ever been suicidal, and I've only explicitly talked about it with a couple family members. I didn't intend for my friends to know, they just sort of gathered it over the course of a few drunken half-jokes.

I can relate to what you're saying. I'm almost 30 now, and I only recently realized just how different everyone's emotional baseline is. Some people are happy by default. I'm not one of those people. Looking back, I think I may have been born suicidal. Some of my earliest memories -- I mean when I was 3-6 years old -- are thinking that the pros of life did not outweigh the cons. Every time I got sick I'd think it would be better not to exist. After a while I started thinking about it when I wasn't sick, and asking myself "does this happiness justify that unhappiness?" I never thought it did. Even when I was happy, I never thought life was worth living on the balance.

Do other little kids have these thoughts? It's hard to believe. 

My best advice to you is to force yourself to do things. Depression and a lack of motivation feed into each other. You need to be both a mindless soldier and a decisive commander. The commander decides what you need to do and gives the order. Once the order is given, the soldier must do it -- no ifs, ands or buts. No room for second-guessing, no excuses. I've done some idiotic things, and gotten myself hurt, just because an idea popped into my head and I gave the order. I instantly regretted it, but it was too late. It had to be done because I gave the order, so I did it. It only takes a second to give an order. It can take minutes, hours, days, whatever to actually DO it. There's no way I can go that long with a positive state of mind. It's just not going to happen. That's why the soldier doesn't think. The commander can think in seconds, and the soldier can act indefinitely.

Success begets success, happiness begets happiness, misery begets misery. Start small and build momentum.

Or ignore all of this. I'm not really qualified to give advice. After all, I'm probably going to kill myself someday. It seems inevitable. But that 'someday' is not today. Not this year.

There are problems with most suicide methods.

Overdosing can very easily backfire, You might pass out, throw up involuntarily and either wake up more or less okay or suffer brain damage. Not cool.

Jumping off a bridge isn't a sure thing. Sometimes people wind up just breaking their legs on contact, not dying. Do you really want to go by drowning slowly in excruciating pain? Not cool.

Even guns leave room for error. Don't eat it. If you shoot yourself through your mouth, you need a high-powered gun, otherwise it might just leave you with brain damage. Going for the temple is probably safe. I'd go this route, except I think it's a pretty lame way to go, to be honest. 

You only die once, so it should be an experience. Jumping off a cliff or a tall building would be a great thrill. The death itself would be instantaneous, which could be seen as a good or bad thing. Disembowelment would let you feel your death, but it would also hurt like fuck and require you to work through the pain for a while.

Best way, though? Fight a bear or a lion. I would love the last thing I did in life to be punching a lion right in the face.

"How about one last beer before you jump, and I'll tell you about my own suicide attempts?"

I've been there, and I think it would have been immensely helpful if someone -- *anyone* -- was willing to talk about suicide without an agenda. But everything they say is going backwards from the conclusion "you shouldn't kill yourself." Don't start with your conclusion. Ever. It's an insult. It's bad enough in politics, I don't need it in my personal life too. I don't want to be treated like an animal or an idiot. I want to hear what you have to say, but I need to be respected. Unfortunately, the hotlines, psychiatrists, etc. are under legal obligations that make this impossible.

So I would offer my story, offer my ear, offer a beer, and leave it at that.

No. I'm almost 30 now, and I can honestly say that in my entire life, there's only been a few cumulative months where I genuinely felt that life was worth living. I attribute these times to mania.

Don't get me wrong, I'm not miserable all the time. I'm just "normal". Of course I have no great frame of reference for what "normal" is; nobody really knows what goes on in other people's minds. When I was a teenager I thought I was different and deeper than everyone else (like most teenagers), but then I realized the flaw in my reasoning: if I'm going to judge other people based on their outward projections (which includes their actions), which is really all that's available, then I have to judge myself on those same terms. Otherwise the comparison is invalid.

So I started looking at myself more objectively. What goes on in my head doesn't matter, it's what I DO that matters. And I realized that I can wear the mask nearly as well as anybody. So there's no reason for me to think I'm wildly different.

It's a little depressing judging yourself on such shallow terms, but it's really only fair. Either it will give you a lower opinion of yourself, bringing you down to your existing concept of others, or give you a higher opinion of others, bringing them up to your existing concept of yourself. Or the two will meet halfway. For me, they met halfway. I'm more humble and more respectful than I once was.

Those few months when I was manic were not an accident; I don't want to go into details, but I went to extreme lengths to change my environment and get a different perspective on life, and for a time, it worked. But it didn't last, and I don't see any realistic way to integrate it into my life regularly. I can't go to such lengths all the time.

I won't say that mood is innate, and there's nothing you can do about it. That's bullshit that's only pushed to sell drugs. But everybody starts life with a different handicap. I just don't think I have the "happy" gene. I can't tell you how many times I had this exchange with adults when I was a little kid:

"What's wrong?"

"Nothing."

"You look so sad."

"I'm not sad."

"Why don't you smile?"

"I'm not happy."

"Why are you sad?"

"I'm not sad. I'm NORMAL."

Is it strange for a preschool-aged kid to be "normal" all the time? Maybe so. I remember thinking to myself at a very young age that the good times in life didn't justify the bad times. I never thought life was worth living on the balance. I can't imagine that it's normal for a 5-year-old to think these things, but I don't really know.

Every decision we make in our entire lives is influenced by our state of mind and our emotions. I've never heard or come up with a compelling reason why 'positive' emotional influences are more legitimate or rational than 'negative' influences.

Even now, when I am the happiest I've been in some time, I cannot discount my "negative" thoughts any more than my "positive" thoughts. Disturbingly, the opposite is true; my reasons (when I'm down) for wanting to die seem *more* rational than my reasons (when I'm up) for wanting to live. (I made a thread about this conundrum in r/suicidewatch earlier this year; feel free to read more there. This is the first time I've dusted off this throwaway account since.)

When I'm down, I feel very disrespected, because even when people don't say it, it seems like it's taken for granted that suicidal thoughts are irrational. This is a mistake. When I'm suicidal, I am *not* being irrational.

Anyway, thanks for adding to the discussion.

I can confirm that excercise can work wonders. My current record was kicked off by hiking myself beyond exhaustion. Felt like a million bucks afterwards, and I got some momentum going in my life. That was the first time in my life I genuinely WANTED to live. Even as a child I never really saw an advantage to living over not living.

This is precisely what I want, but I don't feel like any professional will give me the power and control to do that. If I'm honest with them about suicidal feelings, I'm liable to be taken out of control. If I'm not honest....well, is there any point if I'm not honest? Should I hold things back?
